entries.query:
I build a WebGL2 liquid-glass rendering system from scratch witch language i should use
Imba
Moonbit
entries.answer:
Between **Imba** and **MoonBit**, I would use **Imba** for a WebGL2 liquid-glass renderer built in the browser, because WebGL is a JavaScript API and Imba compiles directly to performant JavaScript with seamless JavaScript integration.  MoonBit is more compelling when your main goal is WebAssembly-first development, but for direct browser graphics work it adds an interop layer instead of matching the native shape of the platform.[1][2][3][4][5][6]

## Why Imba fits

Your renderer will spend a lot of time talking to browser APIs such as canvas and WebGL, so the most natural environment is one that maps cleanly onto JavaScript.  Imba is explicitly built for the web, compiles to readable and performant JavaScript, and advertises seamless integration with the JavaScript ecosystem, which makes it the safer choice when you are wiring low-level rendering code by hand.[5][6][7][1]

## Where MoonBit helps

MoonBit is designed with first-class WebAssembly support and also has JavaScript and native targets, so it is attractive if you care deeply about Wasm-oriented architecture or want to experiment with small binaries and fast compilation.  The catch is that its JavaScript interop is centered on FFI, and even community discussion around MoonBit notes limitations in more complex interoperability cases, such as passing function-typed values in some situations.[2][8][9][3][4]

## Practical tradeoff

A liquid-glass system usually means lots of iteration on render passes, uniforms, framebuffers, and browser-facing debugging, so friction at the API boundary matters more than language elegance alone.  Imba keeps you closer to the platform you are actually driving, while MoonBit makes more sense if you plan to isolate math-heavy subsystems into Wasm and accept extra integration work around the rendering shell.[10][3][1][2]

## Best choice

| Option | Fit for this project |
|---|---|
| Imba | Best overall choice for a browser-first WebGL2 renderer because it compiles to JavaScript and integrates smoothly with JavaScript APIs. [1][5][6] |
| MoonBit | Better as a specialized WebAssembly-oriented choice than as the main language for direct WebGL2 orchestration. [2][8][3] |

If you are starting from scratch and must pick one, pick **Imba**.  Want me to sketch the architecture for an Imba-based WebGL2 liquid-glass renderer next?[6][5]

Yes — if you are open to **other languages**, the strongest default choice is usually **TypeScript**, not Imba or MoonBit.  For a browser-first liquid-glass renderer, TypeScript gives you direct access to WebGL2, excellent editor tooling, and fewer moving parts than a Wasm-based setup.[1][2][3]

## Best default

WebGL is fundamentally a browser JavaScript API, so TypeScript fits the platform with the least friction while still giving you strong types and maintainability.  That matters a lot in a scratch-built renderer, where you will be managing shader source, uniforms, framebuffers, post-processing passes, and error-prone GPU state transitions by hand.[2][3][4][1]

If your goal is “I want to ship a serious custom renderer and keep iteration speed high,” TypeScript is the most balanced answer.  It also keeps debugging simpler because your rendering code stays close to the browser APIs instead of crossing a JavaScript-to-Wasm boundary for orchestration.[5][6][3][1][2]

## When Rust wins

If your project is more engine-like, or you want stronger correctness guarantees for core systems, **Rust** becomes the best advanced option.  Rust can target WebAssembly, and `wgpu` is a cross-platform Rust graphics API that runs natively and, on wasm, can sit on top of WebGL2 and WebGPU.[6][7][5]

That said, Rust is the better choice when you want a broader graphics architecture, shared native/web code, or compute-heavy subsystems, not necessarily when you want the fastest path to a handcrafted browser renderer.  For pure browser iteration, the toolchain and interop overhead are simply heavier than TypeScript.[7][5][6]

## Other options

**Imba** is still a reasonable niche choice if you personally love its syntax and want compile-to-JavaScript ergonomics while staying in the web ecosystem.  **MoonBit** is more interesting as a WebAssembly-oriented experiment than as the main control language for direct WebGL2 rendering.[8][9][10][11][12]

You could also use **C++ with Emscripten** or **Zig**, but both shift the project toward systems-level portability rather than browser-native productivity.  Emscripten explicitly maps OpenGL ES 2.0/3.0 style commands onto WebGL 1/2, which is powerful, but it introduces a more complex build and compatibility layer than a TypeScript-first setup.[13][14][15][16]

## Recommendation table

| Language | Use it when |
|---|---|
| TypeScript | You want the best overall choice for a custom browser renderer with fast iteration and direct WebGL2 access. [3][1][2] |
| Rust | You want stronger systems design, Wasm deployment, or a path toward `wgpu` and cross-platform rendering. [5][6][7] |
| Imba | You want a compile-to-JS language and prefer its syntax, but still want to stay close to browser APIs. [8][9] |
| MoonBit | You want to explore a Wasm-centric language and accept more interop work. [10][11][12] |
| C++ / Zig | You care about low-level control or porting native-style graphics code to the web. [13][15][16] |

For your specific use case, my ranking would be: **TypeScript first, Rust second, Imba third, MoonBit fourth**.  Are you targeting strictly **WebGL2**, or are you willing to design for **WebGPU** with a WebGL2 fallback?[3][1][5][6]
